title: Cap. VIII Resp.: same consequence fails for election and reprobation; negative reprobation is denial of unowed benefit
pass_a_gloss: This same reason proposed by Gregory we dissolved before in the question of Predestination. For in that controversy he tried to prove that predestination is from foresight of works, because few are elect in respect of the rejected. Now he also contends that reprobation hangs upon foresight of final demerits, because many are reprobated in comparison unto those few who are elected. I answer therefore that the consequence avails in neither place. As to what regards reprobation, since it is (as was said before) not punishment, but the negation of a gratuitous and unowed benefit, nothing compels us to confess that God, acting from his mere good pleasure, cannot grant such a benefit to fewer, and deny it to more. We see in the angels that this benefit of election was denied to many, and that without respect unto foresighted demerits: whether it was denied to more than was granted, I scarce dare define. Yet if in the thing itself anything were incongruous, or unworthy of God, he could deny this benefit of election not only not to more, but not even to fewer, nay not even to one, without consideration of foresighted sin. By this sole instance therefore the force of the argument is broken.
pass_b_english: We already dissolved this same reason of Gregory's in the predestination question. There he tried to prove predestination is from foresight of works because few are elect relative to the rejected. Now he contends reprobation hangs on foresight of final demerits because many are reprobate compared with the few elect. I answer: the consequence holds in neither place. As for reprobation — since it is not punishment but denial of a gratuitous unowed benefit — nothing forces us to say God, acting from mere good pleasure, cannot grant that benefit to fewer and deny it to more. We see in the angels that this benefit of election was denied to many, and without regard to foresighted demerits; whether denied to more than granted, I scarce dare say. Yet if anything in the thing itself were incongruous or unworthy of God, he could not deny election's benefit even to one without regard to foresighted sin — let alone to many. That single instance breaks the argument's force.
source_text: Hanc eandem rationem a Gregorio propositam in quaestione Praedestinationis antea dissolvimus. Nam in illa controversia conatus est probare, praedestinationem esse ex praescientia operum, quia pauci electi sunt respectu rejectorum. Jam etiam contendit, reprobationem pendere ex praevisione finalium demeritorum, quia multi sunt reprobati in comparatione ad eos paucos qui eliguntur. Respondeo igitur, consequentiam neutrobi valere. Ad reprobationem quod spectat, cum sit (ut ante dictum est) non punitio, sed gratuiti et indebiti beneficii negatio, nihil cogit nos fateri Deum, ex mero suo beneplacito agentem, non posse tale beneficium paucioribus concedere, et pluribus denegare. Videmus in angelis hoc beneficium electionis fuisse multis negatum, idque absque respectu ad praevisa demerita: an fuerit pluribus denegatum quam indultum, haud ausim definire. Si tamen in ipsa re aliquid esset incongruum, aut Deo indignum, non modo pluribus, sed nec paucioribus, imo nec uni posset hoc beneficium electionis denegare absque consideratione praevisi peccati. Hac igitur sola instantia vis argumenti eliditur.
